paragraphs: When, on the other hand, the provincial governments are given the power to regulate those same affairs of mixed interest, the opposite tendency prevails in society. The dominant force then lies in the province, not in the nation, and it is to be feared that the national government may in the end be stripped of the privileges necessary to its existence.
Independent nations therefore have a natural tendency toward centralization, and confederations toward dismemberment.

It now remains only to apply these general principles to the American Union. The several States necessarily held the right to regulate all affairs that are exclusively provincial. These same States also kept the rights to determine the civil and political competence of citizens, to regulate the reciprocal relations among the members of the community, and to dispense justice. These rights are of a general nature, but they do not necessarily belong to the national government. We have shown that the government of the Union is empowered to act in the name of the whole nation in those cases where the nation has to appear as a single, undivided power: for instance, in foreign relations and in offering common resistance to a common enemy. In short, it conducts those affairs that I have called exclusively national.

In this division of the rights of sovereignty, the Union’s share seems at first sight larger than that of the States, but closer examination shows it to be smaller. The undertakings of the government of the Union are more vast, but their influence is felt more rarely. Those of the provincial governments are comparatively small, but they are incessant, and they keep alive the authority they represent. The government of the Union watches over the general interests of the country; but the general interests of a people have a very doubtful influence on individual happiness, while provincial interests have an immediate effect on the welfare of the inhabitants. The Union secures the independence and greatness of the nation, which do not directly affect private citizens; but the several States maintain liberty, regulate rights, protect property, and secure the life and the whole future prosperity of every citizen.

The federal government is very far removed from its subjects, while the provincial governments are within reach of everyone and ready to attend to the smallest appeal. The central government has on its side the passions of a few superior men who aspire to run it. But on the side of the provincial governments are the interests of all those second-rate individuals who can hope to obtain power only within their own State, and who nevertheless exercise the largest share of authority over the people, because they stand nearest to its level. The Americans therefore have much more to hope and fear from the States than from the Union; and, following the natural tendency of the human mind, they are more likely to attach themselves to the former than to the latter. In this respect their habits and feelings agree with their interests.

When a compact nation divides its sovereignty and adopts a confederate form of government, the traditions, habits, and mores of the people remain for a long time at odds with their legislation, and the former tend to give the central government a degree of influence that the latter forbids. When a number of confederate states unite to form a single nation, the same causes work in the opposite direction. I have no doubt that if France were to become a confederate republic like the United States, its government would at first display more energy than that of the Union; and if the Union were to change its constitution into a monarchy like that of France, I think the American government would take a long time to acquire the force that now rules the French nation. When the national existence of the Anglo-Americans began, their provincial existence was already long established. Necessary relations had been formed between the townships and the individual citizens of the same States, and they were accustomed to regard some matters as common to them all and to conduct other affairs as relating exclusively to their own special interests.

The Union is a vast body that presents no definite object to patriotic feeling. The forms and limits of the State are distinct and circumscribed, since it represents a certain number of objects familiar to the citizens and loved by all. It is identified with the very soil, with the right of property and the domestic affections, with the memories of the past, the labors of the present, and the hopes of the future. Patriotism, which is frequently a mere extension of individual egotism, is therefore still directed to the State and is not aroused by the Union. Thus the tendency of the people’s interests, habits, and feelings is to center political activity in the States rather than in the Union.

It is easy to gauge the different strengths of the two governments by observing how they carry out their respective functions. Whenever the government of a State has to address an individual or an assembly of individuals, its language is clear and imperative. The federal government takes the same tone in its dealings with individuals; but as soon as it has anything to do with a State, it begins to parley, to explain its motives and justify its conduct, to argue and advise — in short, to do anything but command. If doubts are raised about the limits of the constitutional powers of each government, the provincial government asserts its claim boldly and takes prompt and energetic steps to support it. Meanwhile the government of the Union reasons. It appeals to the interests, the good sense, and the glory of the nation; it temporizes, it negotiates, and it does not agree to act until it is reduced to the last extremity. At first sight one might readily imagine that the provincial government is the one armed with the authority of the nation, and that Congress represents a single State.

The federal government is therefore, despite the precautions of its founders, so naturally weak that it needs the free consent of the governed in a special degree in order to survive. It is easy to see that its purpose is to enable the States to carry out with ease their determination to remain united; and as long as this preliminary condition exists, its authority is great, temperate, and effective. The Constitution fits the government to control individuals and to overcome easily any obstacles they may be inclined to raise; but it was by no means established with a view to the possible separation of one or more of the States from the Union.

If the sovereignty of the Union were to engage in a struggle with that of the States today, its defeat may be confidently predicted, and it is not likely that such a struggle would be seriously undertaken. Whenever steady resistance is offered to the federal government, it will be found to yield. Experience has so far shown that whenever a State has demanded something with perseverance and resolution, it has invariably succeeded; and that if a separate government has distinctly refused to act, it was left to do as it saw fit. *z

z [ See the conduct of the Northern States in the war of 1812. “During that war,” says Jefferson in a letter to General Lafayette, “four of the Eastern States were only attached to the Union, like so many inanimate bodies to living men.”]

But even if the government of the Union had some strength inherent in itself, the physical situation of the country would make the exercise of that strength very difficult. *a The United States cover an immense territory; they are separated from each other by great distances; and the population is spread across a country that is still half wilderness. If the Union were to try to enforce the allegiance of the confederate States by military means, it would be in a position very similar to that of England at the time of the War of Independence.

a [ The profound peace of the Union gives no pretext for a standing army; and without a standing army a government is not prepared to take advantage of a favorable opportunity to overcome resistance and seize the sovereign power by surprise. [The results of the Civil War have shown that this note, and the paragraph in the text that precedes it, were a misconception on the writer’s part.]]

However strong a government may be, it cannot easily escape the consequences of a principle that it has once admitted as the foundation of its constitution. The Union was formed by the voluntary agreement of the States, and by uniting they have not given up their nationality, nor have they been reduced to the condition of a single people. If one of the States chose to withdraw its name from the contract, it would be hard to disprove its right to do so; and the federal government would have no means of maintaining its claims directly, either by force or by right. For the federal government to overcome easily the resistance of any one of its subjects, it would be necessary that one or more of them be specially interested in the existence of the Union, as has frequently been the case in the history of confederations.

Suppose that among the States united by the federal tie there are some that exclusively enjoy the principal advantages of union, or whose prosperity depends on its continuing. They will unquestionably always be ready to support the central government in enforcing the obedience of the others. But the government would then be exerting a force that does not come from itself but from a principle contrary to its nature. States form confederations in order to gain equal advantages from their union; and in the case just mentioned, the federal government would derive its power from the unequal distribution of those benefits among the States.

If one of the confederate States has acquired a preponderance great enough to let it take exclusive possession of the central authority, it will treat the other States as subject provinces and will make its own supremacy respected under the borrowed name of the sovereignty of the Union. Great things may then be done in the name of the federal government, but in reality that government will have ceased to exist. *b In both these cases, the power that acts in the name of the confederation grows stronger the further it abandons the natural state and the acknowledged principles of confederations.

b [ Thus the province of Holland in the republic of the Low Countries, and the Emperor in the Germanic Confederation, have sometimes put themselves in the place of the union and used the federal authority to their own advantage.]

In America the existing Union is advantageous to all the States, but it is not indispensable to any one of them. Several of them might break the federal tie without compromising the welfare of the others, although their own prosperity would be reduced. Since the existence and happiness of none of the States depend wholly on the present Constitution, none of them would be disposed to make great personal sacrifices to maintain it. On the other hand, no State appears so far to have its ambition much engaged in maintaining the existing Union. They certainly do not all have the same influence in the federal councils, but none of them can hope to domineer over the rest or to treat them as inferiors or subjects.

It seems to me unquestionable that if any portion of the Union seriously wished to separate from the other States, the others would not be able to prevent it, nor indeed would they attempt to; and that the present Union will last only as long as the States that compose it choose to remain members of the confederation. If this point is admitted, the question becomes less difficult. Our object is not to inquire whether the States of the existing Union are capable of separating, but whether they will choose to remain united.

Among the various reasons that make the existing Union useful to the Americans, two principal causes are especially evident to the observer. Although the Americans are, as it were, alone on their continent, their commerce makes them neighbors of all the nations they trade with. Despite their apparent isolation, the Americans need a certain degree of strength, which they can retain only by remaining united with each other. If the States were to split, they would not only diminish the strength they can now display toward foreign nations, but they would soon create foreign powers on their own territory. A system of inland custom-houses would then be established; the valleys would be divided by imaginary boundary lines; the courses of the rivers would be confined by territorial distinctions; and a multitude of hindrances would prevent the Americans from exploring the whole of the vast continent that Providence has allotted to them as a dominion. At present they have no invasion to fear, and consequently no standing armies to maintain and no taxes to levy. If the Union were dissolved, all these burdensome measures might before long be required. The Americans therefore have a very powerful interest in maintaining their Union. On the other hand, it is almost impossible to discover any kind of material interest that might at present tempt a portion of the Union to separate from the other States.

When we look at the map of the United States, we see the chain of the Alleghany Mountains running from the northeast to the southwest and crossing nearly one thousand miles of country, and we are led to imagine that the design of Providence was to raise, between the valley of the Mississippi and the coast of the Atlantic Ocean, one of those natural barriers that break the mutual intercourse of men and form the necessary limits of different States. But the average height of the Alleghanies does not exceed 2,500 feet; their greatest elevation is not above 4,000 feet; and their rounded summits, and the spacious valleys they conceal within their passes, are easy to reach from several sides. Besides, the principal rivers that fall into the Atlantic Ocean — the Hudson, the Susquehanna, and the Potomac — rise beyond the Alleghanies, in an open district bordering the valley of the Mississippi. These streams leave that tract of country and make their way through the barrier that seems as if it would turn them westward, and as they wind through the mountains they open an easy and natural passage for man. No natural barrier exists in the regions now inhabited by the Anglo-Americans. The Alleghanies are so far from serving as a boundary to separate nations that they do not even serve as a frontier between States. New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia include them within their borders, and those States extend as far west as east of the line. The territory now occupied by the twenty-four States of the Union, and the three great districts that have not yet acquired the rank of States although they already contain inhabitants, covers a surface of 1,002,600 square miles, *c which is about five times the extent of France. Within these limits the quality of the soil, the temperature, and the produce of the country are extremely varied. The vast extent of territory occupied by the Anglo-American republics has given rise to doubts about the maintenance of their Union. Here a distinction must be made. Contrary interests sometimes arise in the different provinces of a vast empire, and these often end in open dissension; the extent of the country is then most harmful to the power of the State. But if the inhabitants of these vast regions are not divided by contrary interests, the extent of the territory may favor their prosperity, for the unity of the government promotes the exchange of the different products of the soil and increases their value by making it easier to consume them.

c [ See “Darby’s View of the United States,” p. 435. [In 1890 the number of States and Territories had increased to 51, the population to 62,831,900, and the area of the States to 3,602,990 square miles. This does not include the Philippine Islands, Hawaii, or Porto Rico. A conservative estimate of the population of the Philippine Islands is 8,000,000; that of Hawaii, by the census of 1897, was given as 109,020; and the present estimated population of Porto Rico is 900,000. The area of the Philippine Islands is about 120,000 square miles, that of Hawaii is 6,740 square miles, and the area of Porto Rico is about 3,600 square miles.]]

It is indeed easy to find different interests in the different parts of the Union, but I know of none that are hostile to each other. The Southern States are almost exclusively agricultural. The Northern States are more particularly commercial and manufacturing. The States of the West are at the same time agricultural and manufacturing. In the South the crops are tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugar; in the North and the West, wheat and maize. These are different sources of wealth; but union is the means by which these sources are opened to all and made equally advantageous to the several districts.

The North ships the produce of the Anglo-Americans to all parts of the world and brings back the produce of the globe to the Union. It is clearly interested in maintaining the confederation in its present condition, so that the number of American producers and consumers may remain as large as possible. The North is the most natural agent of communication between the South and the West of the Union on the one hand and the rest of the world on the other; the North is therefore interested in the union and prosperity of the South and the West, so that they may continue to supply raw materials for its manufactures and cargoes for its shipping.

The South and the West, for their part, are still more directly interested in preserving the Union and in the prosperity of the North. The produce of the South is, for the most part, exported overseas; the South and the West consequently need the commercial resources of the North. They also have an interest in the Union maintaining a powerful fleet to protect them effectively. The South and the West have no vessels, but they cannot refuse a willing subsidy to defray the expenses of the navy. For if the fleets of Europe were to blockade the ports of the South and the delta of the Mississippi, what would become of the rice of the Carolinas, the tobacco of Virginia, and the sugar and cotton that grow in the valley of the Mississippi? Every portion of the federal budget therefore contributes to maintaining material interests that are common to all the confederate States.

Apart from this commercial usefulness, the South and the West of the Union gain great political advantages from their connection with the North. The South contains an enormous slave population, a population that is already alarming and still more formidable for the future. The States of the West lie in the remotest parts of a single valley; and all the rivers that cross their territory rise in the Rocky Mountains or in the Alleghanies and fall into the Mississippi, which carries them on to the Gulf of Mexico. The Western States are consequently entirely cut off, by their position, from the traditions of Europe and the civilization of the Old World. The inhabitants of the South are thus induced to support the Union in order to have its protection against Black people; and the inhabitants of the West, so as not to be excluded from free communication with the rest of the globe and shut up in the wilds of central America. The North cannot but desire the maintenance of the Union, in order to remain, as it now is, the connecting link between that vast body and the other parts of the world.
The temporal interests of all the several parts of the Union are, then, closely connected; and the same holds true of those opinions and feelings that may be called the immaterial interests of men.

The inhabitants of the United States talk a great deal about their attachment to their country, but I confess that I do not rely on that calculating patriotism that is founded on interest and that a change in the interests at stake may wipe out. Nor do I attach much importance to the language of the Americans when they declare, in their daily conversations, their intention to maintain the federal system adopted by their forefathers. A government keeps its hold over a great number of citizens far less through the voluntary and rational consent of the multitude than through that instinctive and, to a certain extent, involuntary agreement that results from similarity of feelings and resemblance of opinions. I will never admit that men form a social body simply because they obey the same head and the same laws. Society can exist only when a great number of men look at a great number of things from the same point of view, when they hold the same opinions on many subjects, and when the same events suggest the same thoughts and impressions to their minds.

An observer who examines the present condition of the United States on this principle will readily discover that although the citizens are divided into twenty-four distinct sovereignties, they nevertheless form a single people. He may perhaps be led to think that the state of the Anglo-American Union is more truly a state of society than that of certain nations of Europe that live under the same legislation and the same prince.

Although the Anglo-Americans have several religious sects, they all regard religion in the same way. They do not always agree on the measures most conducive to good government, and they differ on some of the forms of government that it would be expedient to adopt; but they are unanimous on the general principles that ought to rule human society. From Maine to the Floridas, and from the Missouri to the Atlantic Ocean, the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. The same ideas are held about liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, the jury, and the responsibility of the agents of government.

If we turn from their political and religious opinions to the moral and philosophical principles that regulate the daily actions of life and govern their conduct, we still find the same uniformity. The Anglo-Americans *d acknowledge the absolute moral authority of the reason of the community, just as they acknowledge the political authority of the mass of citizens; and they hold that public opinion is the surest judge of what is lawful or forbidden, true or false. Most of them believe that a man will be led to do what is just and good by following his own self-interest properly understood. They hold that every man is born with the right of self-government, and that no one has the right to constrain his fellow creatures to be happy. They all have a lively faith in the perfectibility of man. They believe that the effects of spreading knowledge must necessarily be advantageous and the consequences of ignorance fatal; they all regard society as a body in a state of improvement and humanity as a changing scene in which nothing is, or ought to be, permanent; and they admit that what seems good to them today may be replaced by something better tomorrow. I do not offer all these opinions as true, but I cite them as characteristic of the Americans.

d [ I hardly need point out that by the expression Anglo-Americans I mean only the great majority of the nation; for a certain number of isolated individuals are of course to be found holding very different opinions.]

The Anglo-Americans are not only united by these common opinions; they are also set apart from all other nations by a common feeling of pride. For the last fifty years no pains have been spared to convince the inhabitants of the United States that they are the only religious, enlightened, and free people. They see that, for the present, their own democratic institutions succeed while those of other countries fail; hence they form an overweening opinion of their own superiority, and they are not very far from believing themselves to belong to a distinct race of mankind.

The dangers that threaten the American Union do not originate in the diversity of interests or opinions but in the various characters and passions of the Americans. The men who inhabit the vast territory of the United States are almost all descended from a common stock; but the effects of the climate, and more especially of slavery, have gradually introduced very striking differences between the British settler of the Southern States and the British settler of the North. In Europe it is generally believed that slavery has made the interests of one part of the Union contrary to those of another. I did not at all find this to be the case. Slavery has not created interests in the South contrary to those of the North, but it has modified the character and changed the habits of the natives of the South.

I have already explained the influence that slavery has had on the commercial ability of the Americans in the South, and this same influence extends equally to their mores. The slave is a servant who never protests and who submits to everything without complaint. He may sometimes murder his master, but he never resists him. In the South there are no families so poor as not to have slaves. From his earliest years the citizen of the Southern States of the Union is invested with a kind of domestic dictatorship. The first idea he acquires in life is that he is born to command, and the first habit he forms is that of being obeyed without resistance. His education therefore tends to give him the character of a haughty and hasty man — irascible, violent, and ardent in his desires, impatient of obstacles, but easily discouraged if he does not succeed on his first attempt.

The American of the Northern States is surrounded by no slaves in his childhood; he is not even attended by free servants and is usually obliged to provide for his own wants. As soon as he enters the world, the idea of necessity assails him on every side. He soon learns exactly where the natural limit of his authority lies; he never expects to subdue by force those who resist him; and he knows that the surest way of obtaining the support of his fellow creatures is to win their favor. He therefore becomes patient, reflective, tolerant, slow to act, and persevering in his designs.

In the Southern States the more immediate wants of life are always supplied. The inhabitants of those parts are not busied with the material cares of life, which others always provide for, and their imagination is drawn to more captivating and less definite objects. The American of the South is fond of grandeur, luxury, and renown, of gaiety, of pleasure, and above all of idleness. Nothing obliges him to exert himself in order to live, and since he has no necessary occupations, he gives way to indolence and does not even attempt what would be useful.

But the equality of fortunes and the absence of slavery in the North plunge the inhabitants into those same cares of daily life that the white population of the South disdains. They are taught from infancy to fight want and to place comfort above all the pleasures of the intellect or the heart. The imagination is extinguished by the trivial details of life, and ideas become fewer and less general, but far more practical and more precise. Since prosperity is the sole aim of effort, it is attained excellently well; nature and mankind are turned to the best financial advantage, and society is skillfully made to contribute to the welfare of each of its members, while individual egotism is the source of general happiness.

The citizen of the North has not only experience but knowledge; nevertheless he sets little value on the pleasures of knowledge. He esteems it as a means of reaching a certain end, and he is anxious only to seize its more lucrative applications. The citizen of the South is more given to acting on impulse; he is cleverer, more frank, more generous, more intellectual, and more brilliant. The former, with greater activity, common sense, information, and general aptitude, has the characteristic good and bad qualities of the middle classes. The latter has the tastes, the prejudices, the weaknesses, and the magnanimity of all aristocracies. If two men are united in society who have the same interests and, to a certain extent, the same opinions, but different characters, different acquirements, and a different style of civilization, it is probable that these men will not agree. The same remark applies to a society of nations. Slavery, then, does not attack the American Union directly through its interests, but indirectly through its mores.

The States that gave their assent to the federal contract in 1790 were thirteen in number; the Union now consists of thirty-four members. The population, which amounted to nearly 4,000,000 in 1790, more than tripled in forty years, and in 1830 it amounted to nearly 13,000,000. *e Changes of such magnitude cannot take place without some danger.

A society of nations, like a society of individuals, draws its principal chances of lasting from the wisdom of its members, their individual weakness, and their limited number. The Americans who leave the coasts of the Atlantic Ocean to plunge into the western wilderness are adventurers impatient of restraint, greedy for wealth, and frequently men expelled from the States where they were born. When they arrive in the wilds they do not know each other, and they have no traditions, family feeling, or force of example to check their excesses. The rule of law is feeble among them; that of morality is still more powerless. The settlers who are constantly peopling the valley of the Mississippi are, then, in every respect very inferior to the Americans who live in the older parts of the Union. Nevertheless, they already exercise great influence in its councils; and they come to govern the commonwealth before they have learned to govern themselves. *f
f [ This is indeed only a temporary danger. I have no doubt that in time society will acquire as much stability and regularity in the West as it already has on the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.]

The greater the individual weakness of each of the contracting parties, the greater the chances that the contract will last, for their safety then depends on their union. In 1790 the most populous of the American republics did not contain 500,000 inhabitants, *g and each of them felt its own insignificance as an independent people; this feeling made compliance with the federal authority easier. But when one of the confederate States counts, like the State of New York, 2,000,000 inhabitants and covers a territory equal in surface to a quarter of France, *h it feels its own strength. Although it may continue to support the Union as advantageous to its prosperity, it no longer regards that body as necessary to its existence; and while it remains a party to the federal compact, it soon aims at preponderance in the federal assemblies. The likelihood of unanimity among the States decreases as their number increases. At present the interests of the different parts of the Union are not at variance; but who can foresee the manifold changes of the future, in a country where towns are founded from day to day, and States almost from year to year?
g [ Pennsylvania contained 431,373 inhabitants in 1790 [and 5,258,014 in 1890.]]
h [ The area of the State of New York is 49,170 square miles. [See U. S. census report of 1890.]]

Since the first settlement of the British colonies, the number of inhabitants has about doubled every twenty-two years. I see no causes likely to check this progressive increase of the Anglo-American population over the next hundred years; and before that time has passed, I believe that the territories and dependencies of the United States will be covered by more than 100,000,000 inhabitants and divided into forty States. *i I admit that these 100,000,000 men have no hostile interests. I suppose, on the contrary, that they are all equally interested in maintaining the Union; but I still hold that where there are 100,000,000 men and forty distinct nations of unequal strength, the continuance of the federal government can only be a fortunate accident.

i [ If the population continues to double every twenty-two years, as it has done for the last two hundred years, the number of inhabitants in the United States in 1852 will be twenty millions; in 1874, forty-eight millions; and in 1896, ninety-six millions. This may still be the case even if the lands on the western slope of the Rocky Mountains turn out to be unfit for cultivation. The territory already occupied can easily hold this number of inhabitants. One hundred millions of men spread over the surface of the twenty-four States and the three dependencies that make up the Union would give only 762 inhabitants to the square league. This is far below the mean population of France, which is 1,063 to the square league, or of England, which is 1,457; and it would even be below the population of Switzerland, for that country, despite its lakes and mountains, has 783 inhabitants to the square league. See “Malte Brun,” vol. vi. p. 92.

[The actual result has fallen somewhat short of these calculations, in spite of the vast territorial acquisitions of the United States; but in 1899 the population is probably about eighty-seven millions, including the population of the Philippines, Hawaii, and Porto Rico.]]

However much faith I may have in the perfectibility of man, until human nature is altered and men are wholly transformed, I will refuse to believe that a government can last if it is called upon to hold together forty different peoples spread over a territory equal to half of Europe in extent, to avoid all rivalry, ambition, and conflict among them, and to direct their independent activity toward the same designs.

But the greatest peril to which the Union is exposed by its growth arises from the continual changes in the position of its internal strength. The distance from Lake Superior to the Gulf of Mexico runs from the 47th to the 30th degree of latitude, a distance of more than 1,200 miles as the bird flies. The frontier of the United States winds along this whole immense line, sometimes falling within its limits, but more often extending far beyond it into the wilderness. It has been calculated that the whites advance every year a mean distance of seventeen miles along the whole of this vast boundary. *j Obstacles are sometimes met, such as an unproductive district, a lake, or a Native American nation unexpectedly encountered. The advancing column then halts for a while; its two extremities fall back on themselves, and as soon as they are reunited they move on again. This gradual and continuous progress of the European race toward the Rocky Mountains has the solemnity of a providential event. It is like a deluge of men rising unabated and driven onward every day by the hand of God.
j [ See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 105.]

Within this first line of conquering settlers, towns are built and vast States founded. In 1790 there were only a few thousand pioneers scattered along the valleys of the Mississippi; today these valleys contain as many inhabitants as the whole Union had in 1790. Their population amounts to nearly 4,000,000. *k The city of Washington was founded in 1800, at the very center of the Union; but such are the changes that have taken place that it now stands at one of the extremities, and the delegates of the most remote Western States are already obliged to make a journey as long as that from Vienna to Paris. *l
l [ The distance from Jefferson, the capital of the State of Missouri, to Washington is 1,019 miles. (“American Almanac,” 1831, p. 48.)]

All the States are carried forward at the same time on the path of fortune, but of course they do not all grow and prosper in the same proportion. In the North of the Union, the detached branches of the Alleghany chain that extend as far as the Atlantic Ocean form spacious roadsteads and ports, which are always accessible to vessels of the greatest burden. But from the Potomac to the mouth of the Mississippi the coast is sandy and flat. In this part of the Union the mouths of almost all the rivers are obstructed, and the few harbors among these lagoons offer vessels much shallower water and far fewer commercial advantages than those of the North.
